cards.text: Grab a seat, friend. This one's a song by Asaph, the chief of the Levites King David appointed to praise the LORD (1 Chronicles 16:4-5), and it's set for stringed instruments. Asaph opens by telling us where God is known.

cards.question: Asaph sings that God is known in ___, and His name is great in Israel.

cards.text: Then Asaph gets specific: God's tent is in Salem. After all my years in the back of a junk drawer, I get EXCITED when anybody has a real address.

cards.question: God's tent is in Salem. Asaph names His dwelling place too. Where is it?

cards.text: Right THERE, Asaph says, God did something to the flaming arrows, the shield and sword and weapons of war. Me? My whole arsenal is a mustache.

cards.question: There in His city, God ___ the flaming arrows, the shield and sword and weapons of war.

cards.text: Then the song hits a Selah. When it picks back up, Asaph starts talking straight to somebody.

cards.question: When the song picks back up after the Selah, Asaph starts saying You. Who is he talking to?

cards.text: Asaph tells God He is resplendent with light. Then he brings up mountains filled with game, big and wild and full of life.

cards.question: True or false: Asaph says God is more majestic than mountains filled with game.

cards.text: Then Asaph looks out over the battlefield. The valiant lie plundered, and they sleep their last sleep.

cards.question: When Asaph says the valiant sleep their last sleep, what does he mean?
True or false: Asaph says the men of might could still lift a hand.

cards.text: Asaph says one thing from the God of Jacob left both horse AND rider lying stunned. Not just the rider, friend, the HORSE too.

cards.question: What leaves both horse and rider lying stunned?

cards.text: So Asaph says it plain: "You alone are to be feared." Then he asks God a question that pretty much answers itself.

cards.question: Asaph asks God, "When You are angry, who can stand before You?" True or false: the answer he's pointing to is anyone brave enough.

cards.text: Then Asaph looks back. From heaven, God pronounced judgment, and the whole earth heard it.

cards.question: When God pronounced judgment from heaven, what did the earth do?

cards.text: The WHOLE earth went still, like a group chat right after somebody asks who's paying. And Asaph tells us why God rose up to judge.

cards.question: When God rose up to judge, who does Asaph say He rose up to save?

answers.text: All the lowly of the earth

cards.text: Then Asaph brings up the wrath of man, all that fury people throw around. And he says where all of it ends up.

cards.question: True or false: Asaph says even the wrath of man shall praise God.

cards.text: And the ones who make it through? Asaph tells God, "with the survivors of wrath You will clothe Yourself."
Now Asaph has a word for everyone listening, and it starts with something they make and then keep.

cards.question: Asaph tells his listeners to make and fulfill something to the LORD their God. What is it?
Asaph says all the neighboring lands should bring ___ to Him who is to be feared.

cards.text: Asaph's song is almost done. He's got one last line about who fears God.

cards.question: In Asaph's last line, God is feared by the ___ of the earth.

cards.text: In that same last line, Asaph says God breaks the spirits of princes. And that's where the song ends, friend.

findings.problem: Stop 2 has 8 story cards and only 7 choice cards.

rule.text: Choice cards are equal to or more than story cards in every stop.

findings.problem: This card cites only Psalm 76:3. It also tells that Asaph 'starts talking straight to somebody,' which is the turn to 'You' in verse 4, so the citation is too narrow.

rule.text: Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

findings.problem: Card 14 says the thing that stuns horse and rider comes 'from the God of Jacob.' 'God's rebuke' is the only answer that names God, so the right answer stands out next to 'A great flood' and 'A sudden hailstorm.'

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike.

findings.problem: 'So Asaph says it plain' makes verse 7 a result of verse 6. The text doesn't connect the two verses that way.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: Most story cards are plain narration with no humor. Stop 1 has two mild jokes (the address and the mustache arsenal), and stop 2 has one (the group chat). Most lines read like a pleasant retelling, not laugh-out-loud Papa Dorin.

rule.text: But he is FUNNY. Not mildly amusing. Laugh-out-loud funny, the kind a baker repeats to a friend. Because he talks naturally, the funny moments come up a lot: in his reactions, his comparisons, his disbelief and his self-deprecation. When a moment can hold a real laugh without muddying a fact, he goes for it. If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.

findings.problem: The card says the Asaph of this psalm is the chief Levite David appointed, citing 1 Chronicles 16:4-5. That reference shows that Asaph existed. It does not show he wrote this psalm, and the psalms 'of Asaph' are often understood to include works by his line or guild.
findings.question: Can Papa Dorin say that the 'Asaph' in a psalm heading is the Asaph of 1 Chronicles 16, or should he only say it's 'a Psalm of Asaph' without saying which Asaph?
